source.title: On the Convergent Properties of Word Embedding Methods
source.authors: Yingtao Tian; Vivek Kulkarni; B. Perozzi; S. Skiena

record.tranche_reason: The study measures representational similarity across independently initialized word-embedding runs, but uses its own dimension-matching and CCA measures rather than the original studies' method.
record.gate_note: The study tests similarity across random initializations for GloVe and skip-gram. It also reports analogy-task accuracy and answer agreement, but those measure task outcomes rather than shared features or representation geometry, so they are not separate rows. It does not test scale, cross-modal alignment, or out-of-distribution inputs.
record.test_reason: The study trains GloVe and skip-gram twice each from different seeds and corpus orders. It then measures how similar the learned dimensions are, using one-to-one bipartite matching (following Li et al. 2016) and many-to-one CCA. This is the convergent-learning question (V3) in a new setting: word embeddings rather than convnets. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add that the authors find sizeable answer disagreement between runs despite matching accuracy, and judge GloVe more stable across initializations than skip-gram. They propose ζCCA as an intrinsic metric that may correlate with downstream agreement; the results are preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes Pearson-correlation-based one-to-one matching and CCA measures for word-embedding spaces; it does not reproduce the original method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported similarity changes with the measure: one-to-one matched correlations are much lower than the CCA aggregate scores for both methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Two seeds reach near-identical analogy accuracy (74.02 vs 74.01 for GloVe) but disagree on many answers (Krippendorff α 0.89 GloVe, 0.79 skip-gram). Higher ζCCA goes with higher α.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Independently initialized embeddings with equal task accuracy still disagree on individual outputs, and representational similarity tracks output agreement.

record.problems: The study uses only two runs per embedding method and one English corpus setup. It does not test different scales or capability levels. Several distributional results are shown only in figures, and no uncertainty estimates are reported.

untested.parts: Scale, capability, and different architectures, objectives or data.
All of it; no vision models.
Whether one embedding can be mapped onto another with little loss on a task; CCA is used only as a similarity score.
Measure settings such as number of neighbours, choice of inputs, and out-of-distribution data.
Plateauing, and whether shared data or objectives cause the alignment (both runs use identical data and objective).
Deep networks beyond word-embedding methods; more than two seeds per method.

missing.what: Analogy answer agreement across seeds (α 0.89 GloVe, 0.79 skip-gram) and its link to ζCCA; a behavioural counterpart to representational convergence.

record.verdict_notes: This is a short workshop-style preprint with only two runs per method and no uncertainty estimates. The one-to-one vs CCA contrast directly mirrors Li et al.'s unit-vs-subspace finding, so the low one-to-one scores corroborate V3 rather than limit it. The V6 support is weak: CCA is by construction at least as high as permutation matching.

versions.untested_parts: Whether alignment increases with model size or capability, including across different architectures, objectives, and training data.
Vision-language alignment and its relation to model performance or scale.
The study tests runs of the same embedding method from different initializations, not broader network architectures, individual units, or feature interpretability.
CCA and dimension matching are used to measure similarity; the study does not test whether mapped representations preserve task performance or incur little loss.
No interpretable features, neurons, or circuits are identified or compared.
The study compares similarity measures, but does not vary their settings or the input distribution, and does not test out-of-distribution data.

The results bear on whether alignment is complete. The study does not test whether alignment plateaus, or whether shared data or objectives cause the observed similarity rather than a common model of reality.

relationships.condition: GloVe and skip-gram, two seeds each, same corpus
relationships.reason: CCA shows a strongly shared subspace: mean canonical correlation 0.74 and 0.66, and near-perfect GloVe correlations in the top 200 dimensions (R3, R4, R6, R7). One-to-one matched correlations are only 21.6% and 19.5% (R1, R2), consistent with individual bases not being shared.
relationships.display_finding: GloVe and skip-gram had mean canonical correlations of 0.74 and 0.66, versus one-to-one matched correlations of 21.6% and 19.5%; GloVe's top 200 dimensions had near-perfect canonical correlations.

source_check.reason: R3 and R4 report mean canonical correlations of 0.74 and 0.66; R6 and R7 establish strong transformed-space correspondence despite weaker individual-coordinate matching in R1 and R2.

relationships.reason: Convergence differs by method: skip-gram is less consistent than GloVe on both measures (19.5% vs 21.6%; 0.66 vs 0.74) (R1–R4).
relationships.display_finding: Skip-gram had lower matched correlation than GloVe, 19.5% versus 21.6%, and lower mean canonical correlation, 0.66 versus 0.74.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R4 and R7 still show substantial shared structure for skip-gram. Its lower correspondence than GloVe does not establish a qualification to V3, which predicts many shared features or subspaces without requiring equal strength across methods.

relationships.condition: one-to-one matching vs CCA on the same run pairs
relationships.reason: The magnitude of measured similarity depends strongly on the measure: about 0.2 under one-to-one matching vs about 0.7 under CCA (R1–R4). The GloVe>skip-gram ordering is the same under both measures, and the two measures partly ask different questions.
relationships.display_finding: Similarity was about 0.2 under one-to-one matching versus 0.7 under CCA, while both measures ranked GloVe above skip-gram.

source_check.reason: R1–R4 show markedly different measured correspondence under coordinate matching and CCA. This supports the metric-dependence component; input dependence and disappearance of convergence are untested.

relationships.reason: Even with identical data and objective, alignment is incomplete: mean CCA correlation 0.74 and 0.66 (R3, R4), and unit-level matching is weak (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Mean CCA correlations were 0.74 and 0.66, and individual units matched weakly despite identical data and objectives.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: R1–R4 support incomplete aggregate alignment despite shared training data and objectives. They do not establish a plateau or identify the cause of alignment.
